subject: mathematics
question_text: If A, B, C are angles in a triangle, then prove that cosA + cosB − cosC = −1 + 4 cos(A/2) cos(B/2) sin(C/2).

mark_split.label: Pair two terms with a sum-to-product formula
Apply the product formula and conclude

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Junior Inter Maths-1A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.41 — LAQ chapter 5 T-Ratios upto Transformations, answer 29, on a ★★★ SSP (Super Scoring Page). Printed appearances: TS 18,19 · AP 17. A MIXED question: the left side is in whole angles and the right side in half angles, so the proof has to cross between them. The bridge is cos θ = 1 − 2sin²(θ/2). ⚠ THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S — no [N Marks] tags are printed anywhere in this chapter (its pages are set two questions to a page in two columns, which takes the margin those tags would occupy). The 1+2+2+1+1 above follows the shape of the split the same book DOES print for LAQ answer 23 on book p.37, weighting the two substantial transformations against the set-up and the finish. The SAME split and the SAME step ids are used on all eight answers in this chapter, deliberately: they are ONE method over different identities — pair two terms, use the angle condition, factor, finish with a product formula. A student who learns that arc once can attempt any of them. The book's chapter header carries ★★ and reads '7 Marks'; that star is the CHAPTER's rank, not this question's. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Paper position: Maths-1A Section C runs Q18-Q24 at 7 marks each, answer any 5 of 7; Q23 is the Transformations slot and is ALWAYS a question of this kind. Re-cut to the 8-mark Section-C form of the 2026-27 pattern (TGBIE model paper w.e.f. 2026-27): the extra mark goes to Pair two terms with a sum-to-product formula.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this identity — say the four moves in order, and where the angle condition gets used.

steps.label: State the angle condition
steps.margin_note: First mark. The halved condition again, because the answer is in half angles even though the question is not.
steps.memory_tip: The HALVED condition, because the answer is in half angles even though the question is not.

recall.must_convey: That the angle condition is written down first, in the form the proof will actually use.
accept: write the angle condition first in the form the proof needs
state the given condition and rearrange it
note the angle sum before starting the transformation
modata angle condition rasi, kavalsina form lo pettali
write down the condition on the angles

steps.why: Without the condition the statement is simply false, so it is not preamble — it is the hypothesis the whole proof leans on, and it is used at least twice below.
common_mistakes: Starting the transformation before writing the condition.
Writing the condition but never rearranging it into a usable form.

steps.label: Pair two terms
steps.margin_note: Three of the eight marks. Three terms will not factorise as they stand, so two of them are combined into a product first. Quote the formula in brackets — the formulas are what the examiner marks.
steps.memory_tip: Pair cos A with cos B — not cos B with −cos C. And cos(90° − C/2) is sin(C/2), not cos(C/2).

recall.must_convey: That cos A + cos B are paired with the sum-to-product formula and cos((A+B)/2) converted to sin(C/2).
accept: pair cos A and cos B with the sum to product formula then convert to sin C over two
combine the first two cosines and use the halved condition
apply cos C plus cos D to the first two terms
modati rendu cosines ni combine chesi sin C by two ga marchali
use sum to product then the angle condition

steps.why: Pairing the two whole-angle cosines is what produces a half-angle term, which is the form the answer needs.
common_mistakes: Pairing cos B with −cos C instead.

steps.label: Use the condition
steps.margin_note: Two more marks. This is where the angle condition earns its place: it converts an expression in A and B into one in C, so that every term shares a factor.
steps.memory_tip: Use cos C = 1 − 2sin²(C/2) so the sign comes out right, and distribute the minus across the bracket.

recall.must_convey: That cos C is expanded as 1 − 2sin²(C/2), which crosses from whole angles into half angles and produces the −1.
accept: expand cos C as one minus two sin squared C over two which gives the minus one
use the half angle form of cosine to convert the last term
cos C becomes one minus two sin squared half C
cos C ni one minus two sin square C by two ga rasta
the minus one comes from expanding cos C

steps.why: The −1 on the right-hand side comes from exactly here. Choosing the 1 − 2sin² form rather than 2cos² − 1 is what puts it there with the correct sign.
common_mistakes: Using cos C = 2cos²(C/2) − 1, which gives +1 and the wrong sign.
Forgetting to distribute the minus across the bracket.

steps.label: Take the common factor out
steps.margin_note: Seventh mark. The common factor comes out, and the condition is used a SECOND time inside the bracket so that both bracket terms are the same kind of function.
steps.memory_tip: Keep the −1 outside the bracket and make sure the bracket stays a SUM, not a difference.

recall.must_convey: That 2 sin(C/2) is taken out and the bracket becomes a SUM of two cosines.
accept: take two sin C over two common and the bracket is a sum of cosines
factor out two sin C over two and convert the sine back to a cosine
the bracket becomes cos A minus B over two plus cos A plus B over two
two sin C by two common teeste bracket sum avthundi
convert so both bracket terms are cosines

steps.why: The bracket is a SUM here, so the final formula will produce cosines — which is what the answer needs, since it has cos(A/2)cos(B/2).
common_mistakes: Getting a difference and finishing with sines.

steps.label: Apply the product formula
steps.margin_note: Last mark. One more sum-or-difference formula turns the bracket into a product, and the identity closes. Write "= R.H.S" so the examiner can see it landed.
steps.memory_tip: The coefficient is 4, not 2, and the −1 must survive to the last line.

recall.must_convey: That the sum of cosines becomes 2 cos(A/2) cos(B/2), giving −1 + 4 cos(A/2) cos(B/2) sin(C/2).
accept: the sum of cosines gives two cos A over two cos B over two so the answer is minus one plus four cos half A cos half B sin half C
apply the cosine sum formula to finish
the bracket becomes two cos half A cos half B
two cos A by two cos B by two vasthundi, minus one plus four
the final answer is minus one plus four cos half A cos half B sin half C

steps.why: The 2 already outside multiplies the 2 from the formula to give the 4 in the answer. Losing either leaves a 2 where a 4 belongs.
common_mistakes: Dropping the −1 at the last line.

insider_note: The MINUS on cosC changes which half-angle form is needed: use cosθ = 1 − 2sin²(θ/2). The bracket then becomes a SUM of cosines, which yields cos(A/2)cos(B/2).
